title: Value Function Approximation
oneLiner: When there are far too many situations to list, learn a formula that estimates value from a few descriptive features, so experience in one situation teaches you about similar ones.

what.html:
A table with one value per situation stops working when situations are countless (screen images, continuous positions). Instead we describe each situation with a few features (numbers like "distance to the nearest ghost") and estimate its value with a formula such as a weighted sum of features. Learning adjusts the weights, and that automatically changes the estimates of all similar situations.

Everyday versionPricing houses: you can't keep a list of every house, but a formula using size, location and age gives a sensible estimate even for a house you've never seen.

why.html:
• Real problems have more states than atoms in the universe.
  • Generalisation means learning from far fewer experiences.
  • It's the step that turns RL into deep RL, and it explains why deep RL needs special tricks.

how.title: Tables can't keep up
how.html: A table learns nothing about a state it hasn't visited. With images or continuous positions, almost every state is new.

how.title: Features and weights
how.html: Value estimate = w₁ × feature₁ + w₂ × feature₂ + … Far fewer weights than states, and every state with the same features shares what's learned.

how.title: Nudge the weights
how.html: For each experience: error = target − estimate; move each weight by α × error × its feature. Features that were 0 don't move.

how.title: Real return or bootstrapped target?
how.html: Use the actual total reward (Monte Carlo: an honest gradient) or reward + estimate of the next state (TD: faster, but "semi-gradient" because the target also depends on the weights). With features [1, 2] and [0, 1], weights [0.5, 0.1] become [0.539, 0.178] after one TD step.

how.title: Building good features
how.html: Chop the state space into overlapping tiles or circles, or use smooth bumps (radial basis functions). Nearby states share active features, so they share value. A single global formula like a polynomial often fits badly.

how.title: Neural networks and a danger
how.html: Neural networks learn their own features. But combining approximation, bootstrapping and learning from another policy's data (the "deadly triad") can make values explode.

demo.html: A walk over 1,000 states, approximated with just 10 numbers (one per group of 100 states). Press Play to see Monte Carlo and TD learn a staircase close to the true curve.

example.html:
One TD step with features. State S has features [1, 2], the next state [0, 1]; weights [0.5, 0.1]; reward 1; γ = 0.9; α = 0.1. Estimates: 0.7 and 0.1. Target: 1 + 0.9 × 0.1 = 1.09. Error 0.39. Weights: 0.5 + 0.1 × 0.39 × 1 = 0.539 and 0.1 + 0.1 × 0.39 × 2 = 0.178.

Supplementary Because the weights are shared, this one update also changed the estimate of every other state that has these features.

misunderstandings: Approximation can represent every value exactly.
With few weights, some error is unavoidable; we minimise a weighted error.
Semi-gradient TD is true gradient descent.
It ignores the target's dependence on w.
An update can make other states' values worse.
Any two of approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy are dangerous.
It's all three together (the deadly triad).
takeaways: Tables don't scale or generalise; use v̂(s, w).
SGD: w += α(U − v̂)∇v̂; MC target = true gradient, TD target = semi-gradient.
Features: aggregation, coarse/tile coding, RBFs, or learned by a network.
thirty: Function approximation replaces value tables with v̂(s, w), typically linear v̂ = wᵀx(s), so experience generalises across states. Weights minimise the on-policy-weighted value error by SGD, w ← w + α[Uₜ − v̂(Sₜ, w)]∇v̂, with ∇v̂ = x(s) for linear functions. Gradient MC (Uₜ = Gₜ) is true SGD; semi-gradient TD (Uₜ = R + γv̂(S′, w)) ignores the target's dependence on w, learns faster and converges to the TD fixed point with linear on-policy features (worked: w = [0.5, 0.1] → [0.539, 0.178] with δ = 0.39). Features come from state aggregation, coarse coding, tile coding or RBFs, or are learned by neural networks. Combining approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training (the deadly triad) can diverge, as Baird's counterexample shows.

check.q: Why do tables fail on image-based tasks?
opts: There are too many states and no generalisation

check.q: Why is TD with approximation called semi-gradient?
opts: It ignores the target's dependence on w
